title: Trump and RNC Report $141 Million in May, Cite Conviction Surge
description_medium: After a New York jury convicted Donald Trump on 34 felony counts on May 30, 2024, his campaign and the Republican National Committee reported raising $141 million during May. They said more than two million donations averaged about $70 each. The campaign attributed a $53 million online surge in the first 24 hours to the verdict, but contemporaneous reporting noted that the campaign’s 24-hour figure could not yet be independently verified in federal filings.
description_long: A Manhattan jury found Trump guilty on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records on May 30, 2024. The following week, Trump’s campaign and the Republican National Committee announced that they had raised $141 million during May, nearly twice their April total. They reported more than two million donations, averaging $70.27, and said online contributions reached $53 million in the 24 hours after the verdict. The fundraising announcement framed the donations as a response to the conviction. The Washington Post reported that the short-window total came from the campaign and could not yet be independently verified because the relevant filing had not been made. The May total covered the campaign and RNC together, not Trump’s campaign alone, and it included the whole month rather than only the period after the verdict. This makes the conviction a documented fundraising catalyst while keeping the campaign’s self-reported 24-hour figure distinct from an audited total.
evidence_notes: Reuters reports the campaign/RNC’s $141 million May figure and two million contributions; the Washington Post explains the limits on independent verification of the campaign’s $53 million 24-hour claim. Replaced unsupported 'record' wording with attributed figures.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Trump and RNC Report $141 Million in May Fundraising After Conviction

title: Republican National Convention — Trump Acceptance Speech (July 18, 2024)
description_medium: Donald Trump accepted the Republican presidential nomination on July 18, 2024, at the party’s Milwaukee convention. He opened with an account of the assassination attempt at a rally days earlier and called for national unity, then returned to campaign themes including immigration, the economy and the 2020 election. Fact-checkers noted that parts of the speech repeated false claims about the 2020 result and misleading claims about immigration and the economy.
description_long: Trump formally accepted the Republican Party’s presidential nomination on the final night of its July 2024 convention in Milwaukee. He began with an account of the July 13 shooting at his Pennsylvania rally, describing how he turned toward a chart when a bullet struck his ear, and urged Americans to unite. Later in the lengthy address he promised a large deportation effort, criticized the Biden administration’s economic record, and repeated his false claim that the 2020 election was stolen. FactCheck.org’s review distinguished the emotional opening from later claims it could check, including misleading comparisons about illegal immigration and taxes. The speech thus combined a personal narrative after a violent campaign event with partisan argument and policy promises. Its statements were campaign positions rather than enacted policies. A transcript of the full address is available, so readers can distinguish Trump’s own words from the interpretations and fact checks that followed.
evidence_notes: The complete speech transcript and fact-checking coverage replace the inaccessible New York Times transcript. Narrowed characterization to verifiable themes and claims rather than treating the entire speech as an authoritarian policy document.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Republican National Convention — Trump Acceptance Speech (July 18, 2024)

title: Trump’s 2024 Conviction Revives Question of Presidential Self-Pardon
description_medium: After Donald Trump’s May 2024 New York conviction, legal observers revisited whether a president could pardon himself for federal crimes. The Constitution does not expressly answer that question, and no court had resolved it. Any presidential pardon would apply to federal offenses, not Trump’s New York state conviction, for which a pardon would fall within the state governor’s authority. The self-pardon question remained unresolved, and discussion of it was not itself a pardon.
description_long: Trump’s New York jury conviction on May 30, 2024, revived questions about what he could do if he returned to the presidency while facing federal prosecutions. The Washington Post explained that the president’s pardon power reaches federal offenses but cannot erase a state conviction; only New York’s governor could pardon the state offenses in Trump’s case. Whether a president may pardon himself for federal crimes remained unresolved and untested in court. The legal issue matters because Trump faced separate federal cases in Florida and Washington, D.C., and a self-pardon could raise a conflict between executive clemency and the principle that no one should judge their own case. The report described an open constitutional question, not a court ruling or a completed act. Trump had previously said it was “very unlikely” he would pardon himself, underscoring the gap between the legal hypothetical and any pledge to exercise the power.
evidence_notes: The linked Washington Post article supports the May 30 legal debate, distinguishes federal from state offenses, and says a self-pardon was untested. Other reporting says Trump had described self-pardoning as 'very unlikely'; the packet does not substantiate a day-one promise.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Trump’s 2024 Conviction Revives Question of Presidential Self-Pardon

title: Trump Distances Himself from Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025
description_medium: In July 2024, Donald Trump said he knew “nothing” about Project 2025 and had “nothing to do with” it, while also saying he disagreed with some of its proposals. The Heritage Foundation’s blueprint called for a sweeping federal-government overhaul, including a workforce shake-up to make officials more responsive to the president. Many contributors were former Trump administration officials, though Project 2025 and the campaign said the plan was independent of Trump’s official agenda.
description_long: Project 2025 was a Heritage Foundation-led blueprint for a future conservative administration, developed with more than 100 allied organizations. Its recommendations included reorganizing the executive branch and changing federal personnel rules so more career positions could be filled by political appointees. The Washington Post reported that many contributors had served in Trump’s first administration, including former Housing Secretary Ben Carson, former trade adviser Peter Navarro and former Office of Management and Budget director Russell Vought. Trump publicly disavowed the project in a July 2024 Truth Social post, saying he knew nothing about it and disagreed with some of its proposals. His campaign maintained that outside groups’ plans did not represent campaign policy, while Project 2025 described itself as independent and said the next Republican president would choose whether to adopt recommendations. The blueprint therefore documents a policy agenda promoted by Heritage and its partners, not an official Trump campaign platform. The controversy centered on its potential influence and personnel ties, not proof that every proposal would be enacted.
evidence_notes: The Washington Post report supports Project 2025’s executive-workforce proposals, contributors’ prior administration roles, Trump’s denial and the project’s independent status. Replaced the loaded assertion that this was Trump’s own 'blueprint for authoritarian rule' with attributed description.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Trump Distances Himself from Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025

title: Trump Amplifies Posts Calling for Military Tribunals for Political Rivals
description_medium: During the 2024 campaign, Donald Trump amplified social-media posts calling for former Rep. Liz Cheney and former President Barack Obama to face military tribunals. The posts targeted political figures who had criticized or opposed him; Trump did not issue an order establishing any tribunal. The proposal drew attention because military courts are not ordinary forums for prosecuting civilian political opponents, and no legal proceeding against Cheney or Obama resulted from the posts.
description_long: In 2024, Trump shared social-media posts advocating military tribunals for political opponents, including former Rep. Liz Cheney and former President Barack Obama. The New York Times reported on the posts as part of a broader pattern of calls to jail elected officials; Reuters later also described Trump sharing posts about military trials for Cheney and Obama. The distinction between amplifying others’ posts and announcing a government action matters: the reporting documents campaign rhetoric, not a formal charge, military order or tribunal. Military commissions have narrow statutory roles and do not serve as ordinary courts for trying civilian political disagreement. Cheney had been a prominent critic of Trump and vice chair of the House committee that investigated January 6; Obama was a former president and partisan rival. The suggestion of military proceedings against political figures raised concerns about using state power against opponents, but the posts themselves produced no prosecution. The reported posts appeared during the 2024 campaign; they show Trump amplifying the proposal rather than announcing a government action.
evidence_notes: The linked New York Times story and Reuters review document reposted calls for tribunals concerning Cheney and Obama. They support amplification, not a formal order or actual proceedings.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Trump Amplifies Posts Calling for Military Tribunals for Political Rivals; proposed date: align with the documented 2024 posts, not June 15.

title: Barron Trump Listed as a DeFi Visionary in World Liberty Financial
description_medium: World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency venture promoted by Donald Trump and his family, was publicly unveiled in September 2024. Coverage of a project white-paper draft listed Barron Trump as a “DeFi Visionary,” while Eric and Donald Trump Jr. were described as Web3 ambassadors. The family provided few details at the launch about how the business was organized or financed, so the role listing alone does not establish Barron’s ownership, compensation or personal financial return.
description_long: World Liberty Financial was introduced in September 2024 as a Trump-family-backed cryptocurrency and decentralized-finance venture. At its online launch, Donald Trump promoted digital assets as part of the project, but Reuters reported that the family offered few details about how the business was formed, financed or expected to operate. A CoinDesk report on a draft white paper listed Barron Trump as “DeFi Visionary,” while Eric and Donald Trump Jr. were named Web3 ambassadors. Reuters’ launch report likewise noted that the family provided few details about the business, and the reported title alone does not establish a regulatory conflict. The available reporting establishes a family role in promoting the venture, not whether Barron invested, received compensation, held tokens or made policy decisions. Nor does the existence of a family crypto business establish that public decisions were made to benefit it. Any conflict assessment requires evidence about ownership, proceeds, official actions and applicable disclosure rules. This account keeps the reported position distinct from unproven financial benefit.
evidence_notes: Reuters supports the September launch and limited disclosure; CoinDesk’s white-paper reporting identifies Barron’s listed title. Removed unsourced conflict-of-interest and financial-exploitation conclusions, which require ownership and compensation evidence.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Barron Trump Listed as a DeFi Visionary in World Liberty Financial

title: Trump Says Military or National Guard Could Handle “Enemy from Within”
description_medium: In a Fox News interview aired October 13, 2024, Donald Trump called political opponents the “enemy from within” and said the military or National Guard could handle “radical left lunatics” on Election Day. He contrasted them with foreign threats and said the concern was people inside the country. The remark was campaign rhetoric about a possible use of force; he did not issue an order or invoke martial law.
description_long: During an October 13, 2024, Fox News interview with Maria Bartiromo, Trump described political opponents as the “enemy from within” and said the military or National Guard could address what he called “radical left lunatics” on Election Day. CNN’s contemporaneous reporting said he was responding to a question about outside agitators and pivoted to domestic opponents rather than foreign threats. The remark prompted criticism because it raised the possibility of using military force against Americans engaged in political opposition. Trump had not declared martial law, invoked the Insurrection Act or ordered troops to act; the available record is a campaign interview, not an implemented policy. The interview aired in October, and the remark did not amount to an invocation of martial law or a military order. The episode is best described as rhetoric about a hypothetical deployment, with its specific target and setting stated rather than treating it as a completed use of presidential power.
evidence_notes: CNN’s October 14 report and transcript identify the prior-day Fox interview and the military/National Guard remark. No source establishes an August 2024 statement or an actual martial-law invocation.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Trump Says Military or National Guard Could Handle “Enemy Within”; proposed date: 2024-10-13.

title: Harrah’s at Trump Plaza Opens in Atlantic City in 1984
description_medium: Harrah’s at Trump Plaza opened in Atlantic City in 1984 as the city’s tenth casino and part of a new wave of casino development. Donald Trump developed the property in partnership with Harrah’s, which provided financing and management. The opening came as New Jersey regulators oversaw an expanding casino industry and Atlantic City sought new investment and tourism. The available official history supports the opening, not the frozen description’s labor-violation allegations.
description_long: Trump Plaza opened in 1984 as Harrah’s at Trump Plaza, a partnership between Donald Trump and Harrah’s Entertainment. The New Jersey Casino Control Commission identifies it as Atlantic City’s tenth casino and a marker of the city’s “second wave” of casino development. A state commission anniversary report likewise records that Trump Plaza opened that year in partnership with Harrah’s. The new casino expanded the resort city’s gaming market at a time when state and local officials were trying to stimulate redevelopment and tourism. The Casino Control Commission licensed casino operators and reviewed their financial stability and compliance, placing the opening within a regulated industry rather than outside oversight. A 1992 report about bankruptcies at Trump’s Castle and Plaza does not document the 1984 launch. The contractor liens, minority-hiring claims and labor violations described elsewhere in the record are not established by the sources cited here.
evidence_notes: The New Jersey Casino Control Commission’s official history and annual report support the 1984 opening, partnership and tenth-casino context. The linked UPI story concerns 1992, not labor conduct at opening.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Harrah’s at Trump Plaza Opens in Atlantic City in 1984

title: Trump’s Castle and Plaza File for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy
description_medium: On March 9, 1992, Trump’s Castle and Trump Plaza filed for Chapter 11 protection as the casinos struggled under heavy debt. The filing followed the 1991 bankruptcy of Trump’s Taj Mahal and sought to reorganize the two properties’ obligations. Contemporary reporting described negotiations with bondholders rather than a 1993 filing by Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts, a company formed later.
description_long: Trump’s Castle and Trump Plaza sought Chapter 11 protection in March 1992 after both Atlantic City casinos faced pressure from a large debt load. The UPI report says the two properties followed the Taj Mahal into reorganization; the Taj Mahal had filed in 1991. The filings concerned property-level casino companies and their obligations to creditors, not a 1993 bankruptcy by Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts. That corporation did not yet exist under that name. Later reporting described the restructuring negotiations as a way for Trump to preserve an equity stake while bondholders accepted changes to the debt; the casinos emerged from bankruptcy by 1993. These arrangements illustrate the distinction between a company reorganizing its debts and an individual filing for personal bankruptcy. Separate reporting about Trump’s later tax losses concerns a different subject; the casino filings are specifically dated March 1992.
evidence_notes: UPI documents the March 1992 filings; later Washington Post and Wall Street Journal accounts distinguish the 1991 Taj Mahal bankruptcy, 1992 Castle/Plaza filings, and exit by 1993. Corrected the false company/date/title.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Trump’s Castle and Plaza File for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy; proposed date: 1992-03-09.

title: Former Trump Models Say Agency Employed Them Without Proper Visas
description_medium: A 2016 Mother Jones investigation reported that three former foreign models said Trump Model Management had them work in the United States on tourist visas that did not authorize employment. A fourth model’s immigration and financial records, filed in a lawsuit, also showed work before she received a work visa. The reporting described workers’ allegations and records, not a court judgment against Trump or the agency.
description_long: Trump Model Management was founded in 1999. In an August 2016 investigation, Mother Jones reported that three former foreign models said they had worked for the agency in the United States while holding tourist visas that did not permit employment. The magazine also reviewed immigration and financial records from a lawsuit by a fourth former model, which it said showed she worked for the agency before obtaining a proper visa. Rachel Blais, a Canadian model, told the publication she worked for the agency from 2004 to 2007; she and other models described agency-arranged housing and deductions from their earnings. A CNN interview with the Mother Jones reporter said the accounts covered models in various years from 2004 through 2011 and that two women said they had been asked to provide false addresses on immigration forms. These are attributed allegations and reported records, not a court finding that Trump or the agency violated immigration law. The frozen 1997 date predates the company’s founding and the reported events, so the event date needs correction to the documented period.
evidence_notes: Mother Jones’s investigation and the CNN interview support attributed accounts of tourist-visa work, the 2004–11 period and related allegations. The company began in 1999; proposed correction replaces the impossible 1997 date and avoids presenting allegations as adjudicated violations.
corrected_wording: Proposed title: Former Trump Models Say Agency Employed Them Without Proper Visas; proposed date range: 2004–2011, reflecting the reported model accounts.
